title: A school of the Lord's service (Rule, Prologue)
word: A school of the Lord's service
hook: nothing harsh, nothing burdensome: a school for beginners
tomorrow: a long list of tools. which one does Benedict save for last?

segments.voice: What is time? Augustine found only the passing present truly here, with memory and hope held inside it. Now the path leaves his book for another one: a rulebook for people sharing one life.
screen: `NOW IS ALL WE HAVE.` → `A NEW BOOK: A RULE.`

segments.voice: A new job hands you a handbook, and it opens with what gets you fired. A gym contract opens with the cancellation fee. So here's an odd one. A rulebook for monks, people who hand their whole day over to a shared life of prayer and work, opens with a single word: listen. Not a rule. A father's voice: listen, my son, and incline the ear of your heart. And near the end of that opening, the Prologue, it makes a promise no handbook makes. Nothing harsh. Nothing burdensome. From a monastery? How does that add up?
screen: `HANDBOOKS OPEN WITH RULES.` → `THIS ONE OPENS: LISTEN.` → `NOTHING HARSH, NOTHING BURDENSOME?`

segments.voice: The answer is one word. We are about to set up, Benedict says, a school of the Lord's service. A school. Not a fortress, not a club for people who are already holy. A place for learning, where not knowing yet is the normal state of things. That's why harshness isn't the goal. He's honest that it won't all be easy. If something feels a little strict, to correct faults or to protect love, don't be frightened and run from the way, he says; the way in is bound to be narrow at the start. Then he saves his best line for last. As you go further in, your heart grows wide, and you run the way of God's commandments with a sweetness of love too deep for words. He's echoing a psalm. In the King James: "I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart." Narrow at the door, wide inside. And here's the detail to tell a friend: on the last page of the same book, Benedict calls the whole thing a little rule written for beginners. The rulebook calls itself a beginner's book. So the puzzle solves itself. A school expects mistakes and plans for them. Nobody arrives finished. You show up, and begin, and begin again.
screen: `A SCHOOL, NOT A FORTRESS.` · `NARROW AT THE START.` · `THE HEART GROWS WIDE.` · `A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.` · then, large: `A SCHOOL FOR BEGINNERS.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write one thing you started and let drop: a habit, a prayer, a promise. Under it, write the smallest way to start again, small enough to feel almost silly. Then sit with the page in your hands, a beginner's page.
A school of the Lord's service. Benedict's picture of a shared life of faith: a place to learn, with nothing harsh and nothing burdensome.
screen: `A SCHOOL OF THE LORD'S SERVICE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold onto this: a school for beginners, narrow at the door and wide inside. Day sixteen-twenty-six, done.

screen: `DAY 1626 COUNTS.` → `THE SAINTS IN THEIR OWN WORDS · 25 OF 80.` → `TOMORROW: A LONG LIST OF TOOLS. WHICH ONE DOES BENEDICT SAVE FOR LAST?`

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Benedict, and some communities read a portion of it aloud each day; some Christians outside monasteries, often called oblates, also shape their lives by it.

Beats from the Prologue: 'Ausculta, o fili' (listen, my son); 'incline the ear of thy heart'; the admonition of a loving father; 'we are about to found a school of the Lord's service' (dominici schola servitii), hoping to establish nothing harsh, nothing burdensome; something a little strict for the amendment of faults or the preservation of charity; do not flee the way of salvation, whose entrance must be narrow; as we progress, the heart is enlarged and we run the way of God's commandments with unspeakable sweetness of love. Confirm each.
Benedict cites the psalm from the Latin (Psalm 118:32 in the Vulgate numbering); the KJV Psalm 119:32 is quoted as the public-domain English.
Carry source: chapter 73 calls the Rule 'this little rule for beginners' (minimam inchoationis regulam); the script says 'on the last page of the same book'. Confirm.
